From the Baltimore Gazette, May 11 1836. Correspondence of the Bulletin. In Camp, Sabine, April 23d, 183G. Dear Sirþÿ In my Inst letter I told you there would probably be þÿ war in the þÿwest. General Gaines has just learned that an emissary from Santa Anna has been in tho ramp of the Indians, and what the result of this will be, we shall see by and bye. In the mean time he has despatched Capt. Hitchcock of the U. S. Army, and a file of 25 men, with

a flag of truce, to the head quarters of the Mexican General, to warn him ol the consequences, and to stay his hand, if possible, from the indiscriminate and inhuman slaughter he is committing upon our devoted countryman. It is not very probable the flag will be respected, but the gallant officers who go on the mission may share the cruel fate of many other victims who have preceded them in the cause of Texas If they do, we betide Santa Anna and his myrmidons ; for the stars and stripes will be untolded in the square of Mexico, when it is hardly anticipated here, or even dreamt of by one of his own countrymen. A call has already been made upon the Governors of the several States of Louisiana Mississippi, and Tennessee, for a brigade of infantry, and a battalion from Alabama, while eight companies of infantry and three companies of dragoons are daily expected to reach here from Fort Gibson ; and if the good of the country requires it, Gen. Gaines will take his life in one hand and his commission in the other, and carry the war into the Indian camp, and the camp of the enemy. To-day we have great rejoicing among the friends of Texas. Last week all was doubt, despondency and gloom ; now þÿw eare full of hope, confidence and exultation. The foolish and fabulous accounts of the Mexicans and Indians, created false alarms and great excitement for the moment, and the frightened inhabitants of Texas, on all sides, were seen flying from their soil. Now they are all returning back again, and official and en-

couraging reports from the army having roused them to a þÿ sober certainty of waking þÿbliss, they will adhere to their smiling landscape and happy homes, and with patriotic firmness þÿ do or þÿdie in the cause and defence of their adopted country. We have seen letters from General Houston up to the 12th inst. He is for the present occupied in protecting the defenceless and retreating families on the east of the Brasos. General Houston has the entire confidence of the troops, and I venture to predict he w ill be at the head of a victorious army on the banks of the Rio Grande before autumn. þÿ Let the volunteer troops hasten on to Harrisburg, by Galveston Bay, and join him immediately, and instead of rifles, arm themselves with good muskets and bayonets which are much needed and are indispensable, and the cause of Texas is safe. Santa þÿAnna army s has been reduced to a fraction. Out of 4000 only, which he had at the commencement of the campaign, 2000 or more have been destroyed ; one thousand are now divided at the different posts, and the remainder will be at the mercy of Gen. Houston in a few days. Captain Quitman, with his gallant troop of horsemen, left Nacogdoches on the 20th inst. He was followed the same day or the next by about 200 infantry, who will be strengthened hereafter by General Felix Houston, who is daily expected with his Mississippi volunteers, and who no doubt will be reinforced on his way by 300 men or more, between this and the Trinity. A SPY IN TEXAS.

From the London Watchman, April 1 3. The new law nttempted to be palmed upon France by the Minister of Finance with reference to the beetroot sugar manufacture, produced a complete explosion on its introduction into the Chamber of Deputies. It is well known that the revenue had been seriously injured by tho two-fold operation of a diminished importation of colonial sugar, and

an increase of premiums payable on refined sugar for exportation. The beetroot sugar manufacturers have profited both by premiums on exportation, and their exemption from paying the duties, to which colonial raw sugar has been subjected. Thus artificially bolstered up, the home manufacture so successfully competed with refined colonial sugar, as nearly to drive it out the market. To protect the latter interest, the government had formed the project of subjecting the beetroot sugar manufacture to a heavy impost, and other vexatious regulations. These appear to have been so much more oppressive than had been expected, that the chamber was thrown into a paroxysm of indignation on the disclosure of the government measure ; which, besides other oppressive enactments, would have subjected the manufacture of beetroot sugar to a duty of lGj francs per 100 kilogrammes. Such extreme legislation invariably cuts its own throat. Bi/ron's Opinion of Matrimony. þÿ An American, in the amusing conversations with Lord Byron, ( New Monthly Magazine), states the following as his opinion respecting matrimony; þÿ A man should marry by all means, yet I am convinced the greater part of marriages are unhappy ; and this is not an opinion which I give as coming from myself, it is that of a very excellent and sensible lady, who married the man of her choice, and has not encountered ostensible and extraordinary misfortune, or loss of health, riches, children, &c. She told me this unreservedly,

and I never had any reason to doubt her sincerity. For all this I am convinced a rnan cannot be happy without a wife. It is a strange state of things we live in ; a tendency so natural as that ol the sexes ought to lead only to most harmonious results, yet the reverse is the fact ; there is certainly something radically wrong in the constitution of society þÿ þÿ the times are out of þÿjoint. It is strange, too what little real liberty of choice is exercised by those even who marry according to what is thought their own inclinations. Dr. Johnson once proposed to have all mal' hes made by appointment of the Lord Chancellor, affirming that the result would be quite as great an amount of domestic happiness as is produced by the actual system. I believe him. The deceptions which the two sexes play off' upon each other bring as many illsorted couples into the band of Hymen as ever could be done by arbitrary pairings of a legal match maker. Many a man thinks he marries by choice, who only marries by accident. In this respect men have less the advantage of women than is generally supposed.

We publish the following important communication without note or comment, onlv recommending it to the serious consideration of our agricultural friends þÿ En. Barb, j I conceive that the planters are mistaken to suppose that an Estate is at all profited by the distillation of Rum ; and in order to prove this 1 will first inquire, from what Rum is distilled ? 1 am told in reply, from þÿscum to (or use the technical þÿterm) scummings, which would be otherwise lost. But sutler me to inquire again, what are scummings/ Nothing I say, but canrjuice, ns valuable as that from w hich it has been separated, and only requiring the process of another clarification, to render it just as transparent, just as bright, and just as good for making sugar, as any other cane liquor: and which clarification could most easily he effected by keepingsmall tubs or pails to receive the scummings as they are taken from the boiling liquor, and emptying these vessels of scummings again into the racking copper previously to its being filled with fresh cane juice from the mill

Again, as regards what is termed the dirt or mud which is left in the racking copper alter the transparent liquor has been drawn off. Anv planter who has ever kept either from choice or necessity, a racking copper of cane juice, (after being clarified) from one evening to the following morning, must admit, if he will be candid, that much less of the thick matter just alluded to, appeared, when the liquor was drawn off the next day; by which I learn that the increased quantity of liquor thus afforded, is just so much actual pure and valuable cane juice secreted in the dirt or thick settling of each copper ; and that whenever the transparent liquor is drawn ofi to be converted into sugar, and this dirt or thick settling is immediately drawn out and sent into the distillery, just so much cane juice, actually secreted in it, is sent away to be converted into rum, which may be more profitably made into sugar ; for if instead of conveying this mud into the distillery, it were suffered to remain in the racking copper from time to time, and the cane juice from the mill successively let down upon it, there is no doubt that by such a process, the greater part, if not the whole of the cane juice secreted in the mud or thick settling of evert' racking copper of cane juice, would be got out by the successive re-clarification. But it is generally said that if this thick matter should remain in the racking copper, it would injure the quality of the sugar. This is merely prejudice and opinion ; for if on some small

estates which are compelled from necessity, having no distillery, to pursue the plan of throwing back the scummings, and allowing the mud from time to time during the day to remain in the racking copper, the sugar which is made is remarkable for superior quality and unequalled sales þÿ the fact remains indisputable, that the process does not in any way injure the sugar, and would hold good in every case, on a large scale, as well as on a small one ; because the proportion of mud will only be in proportion to the quantity of cane juice, whether that be great or small. But there is another objection that in some cases the canes produce such a large proportion of mud or thick settlings, that it would interfere too much in the proper clarification of the liquor, as it would be too thick on the top of the racking copper when newly filled with cane juice. This however only is an excuse, but certainly no reason, why the mud should be immediately drawn off after the usual method and thrown into the distillery ; as in all such cases where there is an extraordinary quantity of this thick fluid, the thicker part at the top may be scummed off, which would at once remove all that was most objectionable and troublesome. There is then no just reason why the mud should not remain to undergo a successive reclarification, that the cane juice secreted in it, might be extracted and profitably converted into sugar; and so 1 proceed to shew the immense advantages which would arise to the proprietor in pursuing such a system, in-

stead of distilling rum. It is evident that if in successively filling up each racking copper with cane juice, the scummings from the taiches be thrown back, and the thick settling of each copper of liquor be suffered to remain, a less quantity of canes will be sufficient to fill the copper with fresh juice, and if a less quantity of canes be required for each copper, a less quantity will necessarily be required for each þÿday w s ork, whatever that may be ; and if this quantity of canes remain in each þÿday work, s certainly there will be an annual increase of sugar, which, with

the sale of molasses, will amply compensate for the rum that will necessarily be deficient from such a process. Experience convinces rnc of this, having given it a fair trial. I had the settling left in the racking copper, and the scummings thrown back as before slated, and at the end of that day, I had consumed in the manufacture of three hogsheads of sugar, 5 loads of canes less than when the scummings and mud were thrown into the distillery ; by which I find that in making 100 hogsheads of sugar I should have saved as many canes, at the same ratio, as would make eight hogsheads more, the value of which would be at a moderate calculation £200 ; and the quantity of molasses which would be obtained from 108 hogsheads, would be 7,500 gallons, deducting 1,860 gallons of which for the general rule on the estate, and calculating the sale of the remainder at Is. per gallon, there would be realized a sum of £300 more, which together with the £200 value of the extra 8 hogsheads would make the sum total of £500 in every 100 hogsheads of sugar, without the distillation of Rum : and 1 will venture to add, that this is as much, if not more, than is usually gained from the same quantity of sugar by those who pursue the system of distilling rum þÿ and it is to be observed, that the various expenses of a distillery are not taken into the account. But as regards the sale of molasses, there will still be a decided objection on the part of the planters who distil rum. þÿ 1 hey will argue that the molasses which is here cal-

culated to be sold at a shilling per gallon, may be distilled into the same quantity of rum, the value of which at 2s. 6d. per gallon, would far exceed the amount raised by the sale of the molasses at Is. per gallon þÿ that is to say, for each gallon of molasses so distilled, worth Is. a gallon of rum worth 2s. Od. may be produced. Of course should such a declaration be correcti it would seem indeed advantageous that the molasses should be distilled ; but it is to bo feared that the planters deceive themselves in this opinion with respect to so large a return of rum from a gallon of molasses. I am the more strongly persuaded of this from many conversations I have had with several planters on the subject. Only a few weeks past I was expressing my opinion to a very respectable planter, that it would be more advantageous to boil the scummings, &c. into sugar as before stated, and sell the molasses, when he insisted that it would be a decided benefit to the | proprietor to distil the molasses, as þÿ lon would produce as above stated a gallon every galof rum ; and mentioned, that on one occasion, on a particular estate, from the molasses of 20 hogsheads of sugar, he had made 1,100 gallons of rum; but as this quantity of sugar would produce at least 1,200 gallons of molasses, here was at once a deficiency of 100 gallons of rum to the proprietor ol a gallon of rum for one of molasses ; besides which 1 afterwards found, by the gentleman's own account, that to make the said 1,100 gallons of

rum he had also distilled all the scummings and mud from the racking copper, which had been obtained during the manufacture of the said 20 hogsheads of sugar. And I am persuaded that if all the accounts which are received through the information of the planters were examined, they would be found very similar to that which 1 have just stated ; not, that I believe for a moment that any one of this respectable body would be wilfully guilty of misrepresentation, but their habit of doing every thing after an old established system, and without any observation, any care, or any idea of a better plan, makes it evident that they

are totally disqualified to give any correct information on the subject; especially too, when we recollect that for the most part, the planter merely gives his directions to those who are even more regardless of exactness than himself, and that he has seldom any ocular demonstration that his orders have been performed with accuracy, and indeed he is generally too much engrossed in the other concerns of the estate, to inquire whether his directions have been executed in all respects to his order, or not. As far as regards the setting of liquor in the distillery, if the quantity of rum which is expected from a vat be obtained, it matters not for all the orders which might have been given in the first instance, whether this rum has been procured at double the expence of scummings and molasses which the receipt demanded ; for as there exists a variety of opinions relative to the quantity of molasses which may be fairly expected from a hogsheads of sugar, and as this too greatly depends upon the soil from which the sugar is made, and as sugar from the same soil will sometimes produce a greater quantity of molasses than at another, from some unaccountable causes, there is a difficulty in exactly ascertaining the quantity of molasses which may be expected from a crop of sugar, so that there is no particular check on the planter to determine whether the account which he gives, be correct, of a gallon of molasses wdien distilled producing the same quantity of rum, and thus it is that the inattention

to the receipt for setting up liquors continues to exist. Besides which, I would ask, how often a crop of molasses is correctly accounted for even according to the proportion which it is generally supposed it ought to bear to the quantity of sugar manufactured. Again, how frequently does it happen, that an account is given of the quantity of rum made, with the number of gallons of molasses said to be consumed in the distillery, but when the said crop of rum is delivered to be sold, there is a deficiency of many hundred gallons, put þÿoff upon leaks, soakage, and evaporation, instead of being attributed to the right cause, that it has never been made. Excuses such as we have recounted are teceived, the old plan is pursued, molasses, which would have sold for many pounds, is lost in the distillery, and thus the product of the estate is rendered considerably less, year after year, by the mistaken system of rum-making. As to the scummings we fear that 50 gallons are more frequently substituted for 30, for who can detect it ? Bum is to be made þÿ a fair crop of sugar is satisfactory þÿ and much of the liquor which may be more profitably converted into sugar, is sent to the distillery to make the quantity of rum demanded ; and the proprietor, while he is pleased with the idea of his rum producing 2s. 0d. per gallon, is not aware that he could have made this without the great expenses attendant on a distillery.

THE WIFE. I could have stemmed misfortune's tide, And borne the rich one's sneer, Have braved the haughty glance of pride, Nor shed a single tear ; I could have smilecl on every blow From Life's full quiver thrown, While 1 might gaze on tliee, and know 1 should not be " alone."

I could þÿ I think I could have brooked, E'en for a time, that thou Upon my fading face hadst looked With less of love than now ; For then 1 should at least have felt The sweet hope still my own, To win thee back, and whilst 1 dwelt On earth, not been " alone."

But thus to see from day to day, Thy brightening eye and cheek. And watch thy life-sands waste away, Unnumbered, slowly, meek; þÿ To meet thy smiles of tenderness, And catch the feeble tone Of kindness, ever breathed to bless, And feel, I'll be " alone" þÿ

To mark thy strength each hour decay And yet thy hopes grow stronger, As, filled with heavenward trust they say, " Earth may not claim thee longer Nav, dearest, 'tis too much þÿ this heart Must break when thou art gone ; It must not be ; we may not part ; 1 could not live " alone !"

From the Cincinnati H hig, May 26. Dr. B. Harrison still living. þÿ Our readers doubtless recollect that the papers have recently been filled with sehocking details of the murder by the Mexicans ol Dr. Benj Harrison, son of Gen Harrison, at a farm house in Texas, in company with two other persons, who were also alleged to be murdered. We have now the pleasure of being able to state that the whole tale was a fabrication, and that Dr. Harrison is still living. This we do on the authority of letters received from him by his family in this neighborhood. The Doctor, however, has had no little trouble, and made a very narrow escape þÿ He was with Col. Fanning's party when the Mexicans fired upon them, and was among the very few who escaped the massacre. In flying from the murderous band he received a slight wound in the neck with a musket ball.

. He afterwards fell in with and was captured by another party of Mexicans ; but on disclosing his character and situation to the commanding General he succeeded in winning his sympathy and favor, and the General furnished him with ahorse, money and servant to enable him to reach the United States. þÿ When he reached the Texan Territory, his servant from some dissatisfaction, represented him unfavorably to a party of Texans, who seized hiin as a spy, and his having come from the Mexican camp and having been furnished by a Mexican General with a horse and money seemed to give strong corroborative evidence of the base representations of his faithless attendant. Accordingly the Texan party carried him on board a Texan armed vessel and placed hirn in confinement where he still remained when his letters were written.

Back, in his recent expedition, a deputation from the Society, consisting of the earl of Ripon, Sir John Franklint and Captain Back, had waited upon the lords of the admiralty with the different views that had been given to the Society upon the subject. On their representation his majesty's ' shin Terror had been placed under the command of Captain Back, to proceed to the Mayne river, on the western coast of North America, near Sir Thomas Ross's Welcome. His first directions were to ascertain the most convenient place for the transportation of boats and stores across the intervening isthmus, and, having placed his ship in security, be was to proceed with the resources placed at his command along the shore of Prince Regent's Inlet, and connect the point whence he will start with Hecla and Fury Straits and Point Turnagain. The utmost exertion is being used in fitting out the expedition, which, it is expected, will sail the first week in June.

SHABBY GENTEEL PEOPLE. þÿ If you meet a man lounging up Drury lane, or leaning with his back against a post in Long acre, with his hands in the pockets of a pair of drab trousers, plentifully besprinkled with greese spots, the trousers made very full over the boots, and ornamented with two cords down the outside of each leg þÿ wearing also what has been a brown coat with bright buttons, and a hat very much pinched up at the sides, cocked over his right eye þÿ þÿdon t pity him ; he is not shabby-genteel. The harmonic þÿmeetings at some further rate public-house, or the purliens of a private theatre, are his chosen haunts ; he entertains a rooted antipathy to any kind of work, and is on familiar terms with several pantomime men at the large houses. But if you see hurrying along a by street, keeping as close as he can to the area-railings, a man of about forty or fifty, clad in an old rusty suit of threadbare black cloth, which shipes with constant wear, as if it had been bees-waxed, the trousers tightly strapped down, partly for the look of the thing, and partly to keep his old shoes from slipping off at the heels, if you observe too, that his yellowish - white neckerchief is carefully pinned down, and his waistcoat as carefully pinned up, to conceal the tattered garment underneath, and that his hands are encased in the remains of an old pair of beaver gloves, you may set him down as a shabby-genteel man. A glance at that depressed face, and timorous air of conscious poverty, will make your heart ache þÿ always

supposing that you are neither a philosopher nor a political economist. þÿ We were once haunted by a shabby-genteel man ; he was bodily present to our senses all day, and he was in our þÿmind eye s all night. The man of whom Walter Scott speaks in his Demonology, did not suffer hall the persecution from his imaginary gentleman usher in black velvet, than we sustained from our friend in quandam black cloth. He first attracted our notice by sitting opposite to us in the readingroom at the British Museum, and what made the man more remarkable was, that he had always got before him a couple of shabbygenteel books þÿ two old þÿdogs -eared folios, in mouldy worm eaten covers, which had once been smart. He was in his chair every morning just as the clock struck ten ; he was always the last to leave the room in the afternoon ; and when he did, he quitted it with the air of a man who knew not where else to go for warmth and quiet. There he used to sit all day, as close to the table as possible, in order to conceal the lack of buttons on his coat, with his old hat carefully deposited at his feet, where he evidently flattered himself it escaped observation. þÿ About 2 þÿo clockyou would see him maunching a French roll or a penny loaf; not taking it boldly out of his pocket at once, like a man who knew he was only making lunch, but breaking off little bits in his pocket, and eating them by stealth. He knew too well it was his dinner. þÿ When we first saw this poor object, we thought it quite impossible that his attire could

ever become worse. We even went so far as to speculate of the possibility of his shortly appearing in a decent second-hand suit. We knew nothing about the matter, he grew more and more shabby-genteel everyday. The buttons dropped off his waistcoat one by one, then he buttoned his coat ; and when one side of the coat was reduced to the same condition as the waistcoat, he buttened it over on the

JDATOas, vffisvasHDBSR Other side. He looked somewhat better at the beginning of the week than at the conclusion, because the neckerchief, though yellow, was not quite so digny, and in the midst of all this wretchedness he never appeared without gloves and straps. He remained in this state for a week or two ; at length one of the buttons on the back of the coat fell off, and then the man himself disappeared, and we thought he was dead. þÿ We were sitting at the same table about a week after his disappearance, and as our eyes rested on his vacant chair, we insensibly fell into a train of meditation on the subject of his retirement from public life. We were wondering whether he had hung himself or thrown himself off a bridge, whether he really was dead or had only been arrested þÿ when our conjectures were suddenly set at rest by the entry of the very man himself He had undergone some strange metamorphosis, and walked up to the centre of the room with an air which showed he was fully conscious of the improvement in his appearance It was very odd ; his , clothes were a fine, deep, glossy black, and yet they looked like the same suit; nay, there were the very drains, with which old acquaintance had made us familiar. The hat, too þÿ nobody could mistake the shape of that hat, with its high crown, gradually increasing in circumference towards the top. þÿ Long service had imparted to it a reudish brown lint, but now it was black as the coat. The truth flashed suddenly upon þÿus they had been þÿ þÿrevived. þÿ Tis a deceitful liquid

that black and blue reviver w'e have watched : its effects on many a shabby-genteel man. þÿ It betrays its victims into a temporary assumption of importance, possibly into the purchase of anew pair of gloves, or a cheap stock, or some other trifling article of dress. It elevates their spirits for a week, only to depress them, if possible, below their original level. It was so in this case ; the transient dignity of the unhappy man decreased in exact proportion as the þÿ reviver wore off þÿ The knees of the unmentionables, and the elbows of the coat, and generally, soon began to get alarmingly white. The hat was once more deposited under the table, and its owner crept into his seat as quietly as ever. þÿ There was a week of incessant small rain and mist. had entirely vanished, and the shabby-genteel man never afterwards attempted to effect any improvement in his outward appearance. # # # # # þÿ Whether our readers have noticed these men in their walks as often as we have, we know not ; this we know þÿ that the miserably poor man (no matter whether he owes his distresses to his own conduct, or that of others) who feels his poverty, and vainly strives to conceal it, is one of the most pitable objects in human nature. Such objects, with few exceptions, are, þÿ shabby-genteel þÿpeople. up in a heated þÿoven. Sketches by þÿ Boz

We have been favored with a perusal of the London, times to May 2nd inclusive, pr. last packet, every thing appears tranquil in Europe, and there is little appearance of a foreign war, a new treaty had been made between Russia and Turkey by which Silistria is to be soon evacuated by the Russian troops ; the payment of indemnity to the former was making and would be soon concluded ; and thus, all apprehension of a war by England and France to support Turkey against Russia is subsiding. Cracow had been evacuated by the Russians, and a small garrison of Austrian troops alone remained, at the request of the Senate of Cracow, to preserve tranquility. Several Ships of the Line were getting ready for Sea at Portsmouth and Plymouth, destination unknown. Prince Ferdinand of Saxe Coburg had arrived at Lisbon, his marriage with the Queen of Portugal was celebrated with great rejoicings ; the British and American Squadrons at Lisbon manned their yards and fired Royal Salutes on the arrival of the Prince; and Were superbly dressed, and illuminated on the celebration of the marriage. Commodore Elliott commanded the American Squadron, consisting of the Constitution, Potomac and John Adams frigates ; he was treated with much distinction by the Queen, and had the station of a full Admiral and commander of a fleet, at the marriage ceremonies. The two sons of Louis Philhpe, the Dukes of Orleans and Nemours, were about visiting 1 ienna, matrimonial alliances are said to be

the object of their journey ; the veteran in Diplomacy, Prince Talleyrand it was supposed would accompany them as their Mentor. An article in the times intimates that the coolness of the King of the French as to intervention in the affairs of Spain ar ises from his desire to be on good terms ivith Austria, Prussia and to strengthen himself by matrimonial alliances in that quarter. In Spain no general action had occurred. General Evans had marched to St. Sebastians which was blockaded by the Carlists ; the British Squadron under Lord John Ilay, had orders to co-operate with the Queens army, in the defence of the Sea ports in the North of Spain. A Duel had taken place between Mcndizabal and Isturez, the two great rival political leaders at Madrid, arising from observations made in debate, after an exchange of shots, without effect, an apology was made by Isturez and the affair terminated The Irish Municipal reform bill had been sent to a committee, in the House of Lords with instructions to bring in another bill to abolish the present corporations in Ireland, and to insure tranquility in that country ; this is considered equivalent to its rejection : a new general election of the House of Commons is talked of. Bills are before the House of Lords, to seperate the political and judicial duties of the Ijord Chancellor,

(From the New York Times, May 18.) Highly important from Texas. Defeat and capture of Santa Anna and Cos þÿ Great victory of General Houston. þÿ We subjoin the following extracts from New Orleans papers received yesterday
©awsk v&8jmrasaj& ra<Mmiutir<M From the New Orleans Bulletin of May 3rd. HIGHLY IMPORTANT FROM TEXAS.

We have been politely favored with the following extract written to a gentleman in this city, from Natchitoches, which goes still farther to corroborate the account received by the Levant, which we publish to-day. The substance of which is, than an express has arrived here, via Natchitoches, from Texas, and is confirmed by General Gaines, that General Houston, of Texas, has conquered Santa Anna and his army. Santa Anna himself and his soldiers all prisoners. The forces of Santa Anna were estimated at 1100 ; and those of Houston at 600. The express further states that þÿHouston s army destroyed half of the Mexicans, and the loss on his side was 6 killed and 20 wounded. The saddle of Santa Anna was taken and brought in, and is of a costly order, being estimated as worth between 6 to 800 dollars, and the express who brought in the news, rode on the horse of Santa Anna.

All this is indeed cheering news, calculated to arouse all the better feelings, which are implanted in the hearts of those who can rejoice at the triumph of freemen over their cruel and savage oppressors The intelligence received early yesterday morning, and which is also published, will be seen to be confirmed by the news brought by the Levant, with the difference only that the numbers of the enemy killed and taken by General Houston, vary in amount.

Head Quarters, Army, April 23 1836. To the People towards Nacogdoches : We met Santa Anna on the 21st; we attacked him with 600 men ; he had 1100 infantry, two hovvitozers þÿ we entirely routed his whole force, killed half of his men, and took the rest prisoners. The history of war does not furnish a paralledto the battle. We had 6 killed and 20 wounded. I have not time or I would send on a full report. I will do that in the course of to-morrow. 1 again call on my fellow citizens to come to the field : let us fall on and conquer the remaining troops, and our country is free, turn out at once, there is no excuse now ; let us do the work at once. THUS. J. RUSH. Secretary at War. I certify the above to be a true copy of the express just received from the Secretary of War, who was himself in the battle. » A. HOUSTON.

The circumstances as related by these gentlemen, are, that the Mexican army bad lor some cause or other been separated into two bodies divided by the River Brazos, that the sudden rise of that river prevented the two bodies from effecting a junction þÿ that Houston marched against the larger body, amounting to 1300 or 1400 men þÿ that the latter retreated, and in their retreat set fire to the town of Harrisburgb. Houston succeeded in overtaking them about seven miles from that town, and made a sudden and vigorous attack on them, and alter some severe fighting, the Mexicans were totally defeated, with the loss above mentioned. The gentleman stated that they were a short distance from Harrisburgh, and could distinctly hear the firing, and that the result was well known before their departure þÿ that Houston had marched in pursuit of the other body, which it was supposed could not possibly escape him,

Coffee, Esq. of the Philadelphia Exchange, has kindly forwarded to us the following extract of a letter, dated New Orleans, May 5, 1836. þÿ Dear Sir: 1 suppose you have heard the report of þÿHouston being s victorious in Texas and capturing Santa Anna. I think there is little doubt but that he has had a battle and been victorious, but 1 do not think to the extent reported As to Santa þÿAnna capture, s it is not so, I am certain, as he was expected hourly at Matamoras when a vessel (since arrived here) left there, long before this battle was fought. It is, however, probable that the report originated in the fact of there being an officer in the Mexican army named Sontano, who may have been taken prisoner. General Green, one of the principal Texian officers, has just returned from up the river, and informs me that there will be a body of 700 men from Mississippi and Tennessee, who will be at Plaquenime to go by land on the 12th May. There will be a body of 1000 or more by the 25th. The seven hundred volunteers who left here for Florida will be back (disbanded) in a day or two, and at least 300 of them will join the Texians, and will prove efficient soldiers. One of the þÿbest officers is here waiting their arrival, to leave immediately afterward. þÿ In haste, yours þÿtruly. DINNER TO Mr. FOX. In celebration of the Mediation of Great Britain between the united states and fka.nce. A number of gentlemen of Baltimore having determined to express their approbation of the liberal course pursued towards the þÿL t n cd States by the government of Great Britain in the affair of the Mediation, took an early opportunity after the arrival of IJenry S. Fox, Esq. his Britannic Majesty's Minister, to invite him to a dinner to be given at Mr. þÿPage s in this city, on the 7th May. Mr. Fox promptly accepted the invitation, and suitable preparations were accordingly made to signalize the event which the dinner was intended to celebrate. The Chief Justice of the United States, the Vice President and the heads of departments, the diplomatic representatives of foreign powers, (including the Secretary of the British Legation and the British Consu' at this city,) the Commissioners of the Navy, the Maryland Senators in the United States Senate, the Representatives in Congress from the City of Baltimore, the District Judge of this District, and the Mayor of the City, were invited as guests On Saturday the 7th inst. the company sat down to dinner at half past six þÿo clock.The table was most sumptuously supplied with every thing to gratify the palate, served up with an elegance certainly never surpassed, if ever equalled, at any public dinner in this city. The liberality and tl taste of the host, Mr. Page, were conspicuously displaved hi the abundance as well as in the matchless

cookery of his viands, in the delicacies which his research had provided, in the costliness, excellence and variety of his wines, and in the rich embellishments with which the board was adorned. The room was decorated with portraits of the President of the United States and of William the Fourth, surrounded each with tiie flag of his country. For the taste exhibited in these and other arrangements of the least, we are indebted to Colonel John Thomas. Mi.Gii.mor presided, assisted by J. Meredith, J. P Kennedy, Dr. Macaulay, and J. S. Nicholas, as Vice Presidents. During the evening the company drank the following toasts ; þÿ 1. The President of the United States. 2. His Britannic Majesty. William the þÿFourth we recognize in his late Mediation, on one hand, the chivalrous courtesv of a gallant nation to an ancient and brave foe, and, on the other, an honorable acknowledgment oi the ties of kindred to a people who have inherited with English law and liberty a claim to share in the early triumphs of þÿEngland s arts and arms. May this sentiment be the sure foundation of perpetual friendship between us and our fatherland. Ibis sentiment was received with a lively manifestation of good feeling by the company, and was responded to by Air. Fox in the tbllovving language : Gentlemen. þÿ 1 thank you, most cordinllv, in the name ot my Government and of my Country, for the manner in which you have drank the health of the Sovereign of Great Britain, and for the handsome form in which

you have spoken of the late offer of mediation. That offer has been nobly responded to by the Government and by the People of America. Wc know that the office of peace maker is blessed through out all lands but bow supremely gratifying, when the occas on is found for exercising that otfice towards a

friendly & a kindred nation ! þÿ towards a people who feel and acknowledge the kindness of the act, and who well know the value of its results ! Gentlemen, 1 may truly say that it þÿ is for the interest of the whole human race that America should continue to enjoy the blessings of peace, þÿ for America knows how to turn those blessings to a noble use. When 1 behold the amazing, the unexampled progress which this country is making, daily is and hourly making, in all the paths of peaceful civilization, noble ture, and in every in arts and in litera- enterprise of industry and commerce When : þÿ I behold these things,, and when 1 reflect, on the other hand, upon how nice a balance the event seemed lately to hang, whether all these happy pursuits, whether all these fair hopes, were not to be suddenly crossed and interrupted by the rude hand of war þÿ 1 feel that it is a just cause for exultation to an Englishman, that the mediation of his Government has been in some degree instrumental in averting so cruel a calamity. 1 firmly believe that so long as friendship subsists between England, America and France, they may command peace over the globe 1 am as firmly persuaded, that a war now waged, between any two of these three great liberal Powers, would retard, and perhaps for generations to come, the general improvement of mankind. Gentlemen, in thanking you for the toast you have drunk to the health of my beloved Sovereign, 1 will add that if ever there was a Kiug in the world whose name may be hailed

with pride and satisfaction in an assembly of freemen, þÿ in an assembly of American citizens, þÿ it is King William the Fourth of England. For already, during the few years that he has reigned, and under his generous auspices, a greater progress has been made in England, in strengthening and securing our free and popular institutions, than during long ages that preceded. As Americans, you are partakers, of you the ourselves, arc glorious birthright of British inheritors together with Liberty, and þÿ I am sure that you behold with interest and affection the present course of public atlairs in England. not You there behold a King and his subjects, madly struggling against each other for a vain supremacy, but a patriot King leading on a willing people in the great march of intellect and improvement ; þÿ a government and a nation labouring cordially together, not to extend the dominions of their country by war, but to render its social and political institutions more free and more popular. This is the great work in which your brethren in England are now emþÿployed wishes of the people and 1 am sure that they have the good ol America for their success. Gentlemen, my sincere and ardent hope is, that the friendship which now unites our two countries þÿ the two great nations of kindred

that our friendship may be as lasting as it is honorable and precious to both. We will all strive and study to cultivate and to perpetuate it. We owe this to our common language, we owe it to the memory of our common ancestors. Americans will not forget that in England repose the ashes of their fathers ; and England will long look with pride and the exulta- tion upon America, as the noblest, firstborn, and the best beloved of her children. Mr. Fox concluded by offering the following sentiment : The United States of America. þÿ May the friendship which unites the two kindred nations of America and England be as lasting as it is honorable and precious to both. This was followed by þÿ Our guest. þÿ We tender him the cordial welcome due to the station he fills, and the name he bears, both deeply interesting þÿ to the affections of the American people. This toast drew forth a second reply from Mr. Fox, which was delivered with much emotion : þÿ Gentlemen þÿ I am overcome with gratitude for the very kind and flattering manner in which you have been good enough to drink my health. I want words to express my sense of your kindness. The friendly, and I may say the affectionate welcome which I have met with in America, can never beef-

þÿTas xasT»333t faced from my recollection. If my conduct, as British representative in this country, shall in any way contribute to strengthen the ties of friendship which now unite America to England, that will indeed be the most fortunate circumstance of my life. Gentlemen, it has been my destiny, in the public service, to he for many years absent from my native country. But I assure you that I have felt, upon landing in America, as it I were at once returned to my family, and my home, and my native land. I have found myself among men same who speak the same language, who have thoughts, habits and teelings þÿ who are the governed, almost, by the same laws arid institutions þÿ who look back with pride upon the fame of the same poets and orators ; in same pages of history þÿ who delight in the þÿ short 1 have found in America another England. Gentlemen, you have been kind enough to allude to the name which I bear, and to the affection with which that name is cherished in America. 1 thank you most cordially lor that friendly allusion. I feel, indeed, in this country, a peculiar pride in being related by birth to a British Statesman, Mr. Charles Fox, who was the truest and earniest friend to America that appeared amongst my countrymen. If we might imagine that the spirits of great men that are departed could look back upon the world which they have left, how it would cheer that generous spirit to behold the America of the present day ! to þÿ see that the greatness, which he often times in the British Parliament prophesied for this

free and happy land, has been more than realised, þÿ to find those prophecies a hundred and a thousand fold filled 1 Mr. Fox concluded with the sentiment : The city of Baltimore þÿ Long may liberty and peace protect the industry and enterprize of her citizens ! General Smith, the Mayor of the city, lose to reply to Mr. þÿFox last s toast, and after some appropriate remarks, uttered with a firmness of tone that showed the vigour and animation of the veteran whose fire Time has not yet been able to quench, gave the following : The floating bulwarks of Great Britain and the United States a host against the þÿ world. May they never again be found in hostile array against each other. The President then announced 4. Charles Bankhead, Esq. Secretary of the British Legation. He has added a new claim to our regard by his efficient co-operation with his own government in the restoration of harmony between the United States and France. Mr. Bankhead rose and replied þÿ Gentlemen, þÿ I beg leave to return you I my best thanks for the honour you have conferred upon me by drinking my health. race that people of America and England, þÿ I am so little in the habit of addressing a public company, and especially so distinguished a party as that now before me, that I must | taken bv Execution from the forcrave your indulgence. 1 assure you that 1 I am deeply impressed by your kindness : þÿaltho I am utterly at a loss to give a proper expression to my feelings. I received with unalloyed pride and grati-

fication the order of my Government to offer His þÿMajesty Mediation s to the President of the United States þÿ and whatever difficulties 1 may have fancied would exist in the fulfilment of that negotiation, they were instantly and dispelled by the prompt and offer acceptance of that friendly reception by General Jackson and his Cabinet. Such conciliatory conduct will be viewed with admiration by His Majesty's Government, and must have the effect oi' healing those differences which existed for a moment between the United States and France, and of restoring to their former intimacy the relations of friendship which have so long united those two nations. I beg leave to propose the following toast: þÿ May the intercourse subsisting between Great Britain and her glorious offspring the United States, ever have for its basis, mutual attachment and good will, and the exercise of a just and honorable þÿambition. After the Mayor had retired his health was proposed and drunk ; and as the hour of midnight approached guests the withdrew. Soon

aths afierwards the company broke up, thus concluding an evening replete with social gratification, and to the enjoyments of which every one felt how important a share had been contributed by Mr. Page.

(From the Barbadian May 18. 1836.) The City of Dublin was thrown into great excitement, and the leeling-- ot the Protestant inhabitants greatly insulted on the 7th of April, by a shameful and extraordinary act of violence, the blowing up of the famous statue of King William the Third, of glorious memory. Some mischievous person inserted a quantity of gunpowder into the body of the iiorse. In the night a tremendous explosion took place, and the statue of the King was thrown prostrate. This aflair is wrapt in mystery. No clue had been discovered by which they could fix on tile perpetrators. This statue which was erected in 1700 -1, by the City of Dublin, in greatful commemoration of their deliverance from Popery and Slavery by the conduct of William HI, was held in great veneration by the Protestants. It had been an annual custom on the anniversary of the battle of the Boyne to go in grand procession to the statue, which was decorated on the occasion, and Orange standards, Ac. were carried ; but to prevent any fatal outbreakings of excited religions and political passions, and in tenderness to the feelings of the Roman Catholics, we believe that for several years the ceremony has been discontinued by order of the British government. The Corporation of Dublin had offered a reward of £200, and the Irish Government £100, for the discovery of the þÿoffenders. Some investigation had taken place, but nothing of importance had been elicited.

The exciting subject of the abolition of military flogging has received its quietus for a time. Major Faneourt made a motion þÿ that it is the opinion of this House the punishment of flogging should be entirely abolished in the British þÿArmy. This was opposed by his þÿMajesty s ministers, and by several of the most experienced military men. The opinion of the Duke of Wellington, after a most minute inquiry before a Committee of the Legislature, and a variety of questions put to his Grace, bearing upon the subject in every possible shape, has doubtless had its due influence on the government, for who, in the whole compass of the British Army is so well qualified, from experience and from diligent observation, and deep reflection, to judge of the expediency of the measure ? His Grace, and almost every officer of any distinction is of the same opinion, declared that the discipline and eflectiveness of the army could not be maintained by the adoption of any other mode of punishment. Major þÿFancourt motion s was put to the vote and negatived majority of 17 þÿ against it. Lady Fitz Patrick had once been the most celebrated beauty of her day, and having preserved her sylph like figure and bright hazel eyes, lighted up with the assistance of rouge , she still maintained an opinion, that to feel young was the same as to be young ; therefore her costume was as juvenile as ever. She disdained the use of the caps or turbans, but wore her dark hair dressed with jewels, and piqued herself upon leading the þÿ best dressed þÿlife in the world of fashion, where existence itself seemed to her a joyous carnival of continued and uninterrupted festivity. Her whole time and thoughts were engrossed in preparing to receive visitors, and in attracing admiration when they came. She was all fascination for strangers ; but unfortunately, the more nearly people were connected with her, the less she cared for their good opinion ; her heart might be compared to a well-frequented hotel, where the last comers were always the most welcome ; her conversation, her music, her dress, and her smiles, were all put on, like her diamonds, for public display ; but when her husband or family wished to share in private what was so lavishly bestowed on every one else, she complained of being languid, nervous, indisposed, or any thing that gave her an excuse for being indolent and ennuyee. In short, this lady was as she wished to be, the idol of all her mere general acquaintances, who remarked with astonishment and disapprobation how carelessly Sir Richard listened to their rapturous praises of her lively and cap-

tivating manners, and how immediately he turned off the subject when the grace and vivacity of his wife became, as it frequently did, the topic of an unqualified panegyric. þÿ Sir Richard Fitz- Patrick was an easy, indolent man, fond of good eating and luxurious living, who often found his own table in such a racket of confusion, or else so delivered up to dulness, that lie dined frequently at the club when lie could escape from home ; and his children only saw their mother when they were fantastically dressed in the evening, in order to display their various accomplishments like so many little fantoccini, for the amusement of the company. Lady Fitz- þÿPatrick s house was the surest avenue to good society in Edinburgh; and whatever individual was introduced by her, might be as certain of rapid circulation as a new shilling out of the mint. Her house was lighted up for company twice every week, and no one else presumed to be þÿ at þÿhome on the nights when her parties took place. She was lady-patron-

AW5ess of every public ball that was given during the season ; she could fill the theatre, on a þÿday s notice, with a numerous and fashionable audience ; and her table was covered every morning, like a snow-storm, with cards and invitations, so that she often languishly threatened to give up residing in Edinburgh, to avoid the trouble of answering notes, or else to appoint a secretary of her own for the home department.

CHRISTIANSTED, 4th JULY 1836. 0 0 By the 2nd May packet London papers to 15th of that month are received, the following extrao.is are from the London Times: BATTLE BEFORE ST. SEBASTIANS. St- Sebastians May 6. Yesterday was a glorious day for the British Legion and the þÿQueen s cause. Lieutenant General Evans had just arrived from St. Ander, (from whence the Legion had been conveyed to this place by Steamers), and the whole had not yet arrived, when the General decided, on attacking the þÿenemy s strong works in front of this town. Yesterday at two þÿo clockin the morning the whole ol the troops about 6,000 men marched out of the town ; at three þÿo clock they were in front of the enemies lines which were very strong, and which they had been 4 months in fortifying ; nature and art had combined to render them very formidable. The troops were ibrmed in three columns of attack, each headed by their respective Generals, the first lines were soon carried ; but at the second lines the enemy made a most determined resistance ; and kept up a most deadly fire upon our troops, and for a length of time beat them back, and they were long exposed to a terrible fire þÿ how the Lieut. General escaped at this moment is a miracle, he commanded tiie centre column, which met with the greatest resistance ; but ho was seen, hat in hand, waving forward his troops in the hottest of the lire; the steep ascent and muddy state of the ground, nearly knee deep from the late rains, gave the enemy, who fought under

cover of his works, a great advantage þÿ the battle had now lasted six hours. The Phenix and Salamander Steamers which had just arrived with the 4th and 8th regiments on board, (1300 men) immediately disembarked them, and in ten minutes from their landing, they were marching to the assistance of their countrymen in columns of attack, with fixed bayonets. The Phenix and Salamander took up a position which enabled them to open their fire, with effect, on the þÿenemy s line ; and they threw their shells with such precision (a distance of 1500 yards), as to destroy the epaulment of the þÿenemy w s orks, and to effect a breach, þÿthro which our men entered, the Lieut. General himself heading the 4th and 8th regiments, which carried the redoubts at the point of the bayonet; immediately the whole of their second lines of works were þÿcarried the whole of the population of St Sebastians were on Castle Hill, cheering the þÿtroops the enemy abandoned all his works, and þÿretreated the latter have since been destroyed. The British loss is severe ; 800 killed and wounded, among whom are 60 to 70 officers, but the character of British soldiers was well

The Toulon fleet had been strengthened by three Ships of the line from Brest, it is called a fleet of observation. TRUTH IS STRANGE, STANGER THAN þÿFICTION. ( From the Georgia Sentinel.) This line of Byron's was never better illustrated than by the following narrative of facts from the Georgia Sentinel. If the circumstances, here recorded, had been interwoven into a popular novel, critic and reader both would have pronounced them the most improbable that were ever engendered in the imagination of man. The paper from which it is taken may well call it a þÿ singular circumþÿstance. Nat. Eagle. þÿ Some time during the year of 1815, Mr. Henry Lossley, of Georgia, the son of a gentleman of moderate circumstances, was married to Miss Mary Lansing, a lady of some accomplishments and great personal beauty. A few months after their union, it became evident that they would have to gain support by actual labor ; and it was certain that in Georgia they could not do more than obtain a mere subsistence. It was thought best that Mr. Lossley should travel into some new country, get piece a of land, make some little improvements on it, and then return to carry out his companion. Mr L. travelled to the State of Kentucky, and was about contracting for a piece of land in the neighbourhood of where the town of H. is now built. He availed himself of the first opportunity of writing a few lines to his companion. This letter never reached the beloved object for whom it was intended þÿ but fell into the hands of one with whom Mr. Lossley had been a competitor. An answer came þÿ but not of Mrs Lossley, but apparently from her father, with whom he had left her during

his absence. þÿ Dear Son. þÿ Your wife took sick about a week after your departure. At first we did not entertain fears concerning her. After some days her brain became affected, and she lost her reason, and while in this situation, she called every one who was in attendance on her. þÿ Henry þÿ! A short time before her death, she came to herself, and seemed to have but one desire to live, which was to see you ! and her last sentence was þÿ Oh my dear Henry ! and shall 1 see him no more in this life þÿ! and breathed her þÿlast. On the reception of this letter Mr. Lossley became almost desperate. His whole amount of earthly goods seemed to be cut off at one stroke. He made several attempts to answer the letter, but found it impossible to write on such a painful subject. He became a solitary man þÿ being in the land of strangers þÿ and had no person to whom he could unbosom himself, and though grief is fond of company, yet he had to share his alone. The thought of returning to the place where he had so often beheld the fair face and lovely form of his now lost Mary, without being able to sec her, he could not bear, and having left but little behind save his companion, that was of any consequence to him, he gave up the idea of returning. Neither had he any disposition to settle himself ; and finding that fie could sustain his grief better when travelling than any other way,, he joined himself to a company of fur traders, and shaped his course to the Rocky Mountains, lie passed nearly two

years among the North Western Indians. þÿ The hardships he endured, the dangers through which he passed, ail had a tendency to call off his mind from former sorrow, and by the time he had returned to Missouri he had in some degree obtained his former

cheerfulness. The roll of years at length wore away his grief, and finding at last an object on which he could place his afTection he again married. From the time that he left his companion in Georgia till lie married his second wife, it was about five years. But what shall we say about Mrs. Lossley ; for strange to tell, she yet lived ! Weeks, months, and years passed by, but had brought her no tidings of her absent husband. Rost Officers were examined, but no letter came. His name was looked for in the public prints, but could not be found. Travellers were enquired of but to no avail. Not a word could she hear of him. At length she gav-_ him up as dead, and conceived of his deal in many ways. After a lapse of seven long years and more, after the departure of Mr. Lossley, Mr. .Stark offered his hand in marriage to Mrs. Lossley; and as it was firmly believed by herself and friends that he was dead, she accepted. At this time Mr. Lossley was living in the state of Missouri, where he continued to live for something like 18 years. About 14 years after his marriage, his second wife died þÿ and he was left with 2 children, a son and a daughter. The daughter was the eldest, and took charge of her þÿfather house s þÿ but a little more than 3 years after the death of her mother, she married, and moved to North Alabama, and her father and brother went with her. In the mean time Mrs Stark had lost her husband and father, and having but one child, and that a little daughter, she moved to North

Alabama also, to live with an used uncle, who was living in that part of the country ; so that Mr. Lossley and Mrs. Stark became neighbours þÿ and they became acquainted with each other as Gol. Lossley (this title he had obtained when among the fur traders,) and Mrs. Stark. T hey formed an attachment for each other; and Colonel Looslcy eventually offered her his hand in marriage, which she accepted. It is to be observed that during the whole of their intercourse they took great care never to mention any circumstances connecting-itself with their first marriage, and both passed as having been married but once; they had both been so very cautious on this subject that the slightest trace of their former acquaintance was not discovered until the night before the marriage was to have been solemnized. The night before the marriage, as they were conversing alone, the Colonel remarked that he expected to be a little frightened the next evening þÿ saving, with him the older the worse þÿ þÿ þÿfor, said he, þÿ when I married the first time, I was not so much embarrassed as when I married the þÿlast? to which Mrs. Stark replied bv saying, þÿ You have been married twice it þÿseems, The Colonel tried at first to change the subject of tbe conversation, but soon found that would not do ; and knowing it would have come out, sooner or later, he went into a detail of all the circumstances connected with the first marriage, giving names and dates ! This was a subject on which the Colonel was eloquent. At

length, looking upon his intended bride, he saw that she had been taking more than usual interest in the relation he had been making, lie then broke silence by saying þÿ you must forgive me for the kind remembrance 1 bear for the beloved companion of my þÿyouth. þÿ While ho was uttering this sentence, Mrs. Stark swooned away, and would have fallen from her seat had not the Colonel supported her. While she lay in this deathlike slate

many were the reflections which passed through the mind of the Colonel. First supposing that as he had for a time kept this a secret from her, and at last divulging it without intending to do so, it might have a tendency to destroy her confidence in him, or cause her to fear that his affections were so much placed upon the memory of his first wife, that it would be impossible for him to respect her as he ought ; these and many other thoughts of a like kind rushed through his mind, and he but wanted the power of utterance on the part of Mrs. Stark to hear her renounce him for ever But oh ! how mistaken were his fears. No sooner was she roused from her swoon than she threw her arms aiound his neck, and resting her head upon his bosom, sobbed like a child, crying out, þÿ Oh ! my husband þÿ! The Colonel being much astonished, inquired rather hastily what she meant ? With her hands still resting upon his shoulder with a countenance beaming with joy, and suffused with tears þÿ she exclaimed, with a half choked utterance, þÿ I am your long lost Mary ! and you are my Henry, whom 1 have mourned as dead these twenty years. The joy became mutual. That night and the next day were spent in relating circumstances which transpired with them during their seperation, and admiring the Providence that brought them together. On the next evening those bidden to the marriage attended. The Parson came, but there was no service for him to render. The transported couple informed the assembly that they had
been lawfully married upwards of twenty years before and gave a brief outline of their history, and entered into the hiliarity of the evening with a degree of cheerfulness unusual to them both.

Maketii known : that whereas it has come to my knowledge, that the law issued against cockfights has been transgressed, the violation of which, independent of its illegality, might easily he productive of much disorder and mischief, being however unwilling to deprive the inhabitants entirely of an amusement to which they have been so long accustomed, 1 have deemed it expedient to prescribe certain restrictions, bv which those meetings shall in future, be regulated: I do, therefore, hereby direct and order as follows : þÿ 1. No cockfight shall henceforward take place in the island of St. Croix, whether in town or country, without a special permission from the Governor General ; which permission however will not he granted, unless a petition to that purpose be presented signed by two

burghers residing in the island, thereby making themselves responsible for any irregularities, which the said cockfight might occasion. 2. Previous to a cockfight taking place, the above mentioned permission shall be exhibited to the master of police in whose jurisdiction, it is intended to be held, and notice given to him with regard to the appointed time and place for it. This officer shall then certify by his signature the said permission, that it has been duly presented to him. It shall, furthermore, be produced to, and signed by the proprietor, administrator, or inhabitant of the premises, selected for the cockfight. This individual, in granting the use of his premises for the aforesaid purpose, incurs the same responsibility as mentioned under 1. 3. For permission to hold a cockfight 25 Ps. shall be paid to the poor; 5 Ps. to the master of police for his certificate and whenever a cockfight is held in eitheir of the towns also 5 Ps. to the police servants ot whom two shall there invariably be present. 4. Those who, in accordance with 1 & 2, take upon themselves the responsibility attending on a cockfight, whose duty it therefore is, to see that peace and good order be maintained, shall, in case of riots or any other illegal proceedings arising from it be subject to a penalty of from 5 to 100 Ps. according to circumstances, exclusive of all other consequences to which their conduct may subject them. 5. Any free person holding a cockfight without due observance of these present regula-

tions or who allows or connives at the same being held at my place, either belonging to, or occupied by him or otherwise under his charge, shall he fined from 20 to 100 1's. and all persons found joining in such illegal meetings shall be fined from 5 to 50 Ps. as circumstances may dictate. G. All cocks found at meetings held in contravention with the tenor of tlii< proclamation shall be confiscated, and sold for the benefit of the poor, as likewise all fines herein mentioned, shall devolve to thein where no informer exists, otherwise the informer shall be entitled to the one half thereof.

Transgressions of these orders shall he decided by the court of police for that jurisdiction wherein they are committed ; the offenders to pay all legal charges and fees connected there with in pursuance with the regulations. 8. Persons not free, convicted of violation of the above orders shall suffer corporal punishment according to circumstances. According to the above mentioned regulations all concerned have to conform themselves. The remarkable teaturc in our society is the co-existence of wealth, want and idleness : of wealth which does not relieve want; of capital which does not employ labor : that men having their heads and hands unemployed, should not make for themselves food and clothing ; that we should have at once a patrician and a pauper aristocracy, but dependent upon the industry which intervenes and divides them : that the generality of men cannot live by industry, cannot raise themselves to independence, cannot of themselves exert the energies given them by nature, cannot work and defy the world, but must perforce cling to the skirts of some friend, some patron, some benefactor, or else sink into idleness and starvation : that those who are employed should live by offices and cares for the concerns of others, and not by increasing production. It is not so in America : there men stand by the force of individual strength, by the exercise of individual energy, they stand and prosper, and can defy their neighbors and the world. Yet they enjoy the advantages of society, and the subdivision of labor, and each man takes to him a rateable share of the surplus which subdivision enables society to produce. This is the condition of freedom and of nature.

What is the alkali by which society is blended? Free industry þÿ free competition for property, and the produce of labor. What acid has neutralized its power, and decomposed society in England? Taxation. Yet we have 800 millions of funded property. Why do men bury tiicir capital in the funds, instead of employing it in conjunction with labor? þÿ This is the deception. The funds are but the mirage of wealth, a complex means by which one man is enabled to live on the labor of another Men often think that when they put money in the funds, they add to the riches of the state, and ask how capital coula be employed if there were no funds They do not remember that when A buys in, B sc:Is out ; said, that money accumulates in 'a gc n : the money is not left in idleness. It evsis in appearance, but the appearance is occasioned by the deficiency and not by the means ; by debt and not by assets. The national debt is a means by wuich on' mar. is enabled to consume ilie produce ot another man's labor, therefore the one i« master, the other is servant. CHRISTIAN STED, AUGUST 25, 1836. NEW YORK AUGUST, 1. The war in Texas is not finished; it is on the point of being renewed with redoubled fury. Hatred against Texas has become national and general in Mexico. General Filosola will perhaps lose his head for the retreat he made, by the command of Santa Anna. The Texian commissioners sent to treat for the exchange of Prisoners, bearing Santa Anna's protection and passport, have been seized, and put in Irons. An army of 7,000 Mexicans is advancing under General Urrea, the Texian army, about 3,000 men ( mostly Rijles,) had advanced to the Southern Frontier of Texas, they are now commanded by General Lamar, as General Houston had not been able to resume the command, but remained at Nacodochez, confined by his wound. Santa Anna is in Irons, in consequence of the treatment received by the Texian commissioners ; he is strongly guarded ; great efforts will be made by the Mexicans to recapture him. It is said the advancing Mexican army had already lost most of their horses, stolen by the Camancho Indians, in the night, while turned out to graze in the Prairies. In addition to Urrca's army, another of equal force is said to be forming, to follow the former, but such a dread of the Rifle exists among the Mexican soldiers, that it will be difficult to get them to face this formidable and favorite weapon of the west.

quake accompanied by an unusually loud rumbling noise, was experienced. The motion appeared to be scillatory, rather than the waVe like movement which is generally observable in these concussions. þÿ From the St. Thomas Times, August 13.

From the Caledonian Mercury, July 11. Letters and papers have been received from Madrid to the 30th ult, and St. Sebastian to the 28th, but they bring accounts very little favourable to the cause of the Queen. Cordova, if he is indeed honest in that cause, which has been long suspended, has shown himself at least incapable of the post he holds. It is evident that he looks with a jealous eye on the British legion, and has never heartily co-operated with General Evans, who, it is said, will not remain much longer in Spain, as he feels himself and his troops to have been ill used on all sides and by all parties. This is perhaps just what Cordova would wish ; as it is more than insinuated that the presence of the legion is the only obstacle w hich prevents him from selling his country, and placing his old despotic master on the Throne. A Carlist expedition, which has penetrated into the Asturias, seems, by the accounts in the Paris journals, to have been successful. It has defeated the Christines, Cabrera, it is stated, is to receive a large supply of clothing and ammunition, which will make his already numerous band very efficient. Even Victoria is again threatened by the Carlists, and Cordova, who lias marched towards it, does as little now, or less, than before he went to the capital. The inhabitants of Madrid appear to the wholly occupied with the intrigues of the present Administration to influence the elections, and altogether indifferent to the fate oi the war. lsturitz, it is said, is very san-

guine success, and calculates on a majority of of about 30 Deputies, and an overwhelming majority in the Upper Chamber. From the same, July 14. We have inserted various private letters from Spain. We regret to observe that those from St. Sebastian state, that discontent prevails in the British Eegion, and that many resignations of officers have taken place. The letters from Purcclona mention, that the Veteran Mina has recovered Iris health, and is again active in the field. It is indeed surprising to see the contrast between iiis success with Iiis small army, and that of Cordova with the immense force under his command. M:na lias been already able to destroy and capture the active Carlist chiefs Torres, Montiola, fSorur, and Borges. The band of the priest Tristany was, at the date of the letters, closely pursued and routed by Gurrea. Many of the C'arlists itavc laid down their arms, and have been pardoned and sent to their homes by Mina. In fact, as far as the Catalonian province is concerned, the most sanguine hopes are entertained that not a single Cailist band will exist there by the end of August. The Paris papers contain letters and extracts from the Madrid papers up to the 3d. The Isturitz Ministry still held out at Madrid, but the capital was in consternation on account of the reverses which the Queen's troops had suflcred, some of which were known at Madrid. The only favourable news to the Queen's cause which they contain, is a report that the Carlists, who have entered the Astu-
rias, are surrounded by Espartcro's troops, but this seems doubtful.

We have been favored with London papers to 15th July inclusive pr last packet, their contents arc not very interesting : þÿ Alibaud, convicted of an attempt to kill the King, was guillotined at Parison the 11th July, lie made no attempt to palliate or deny the charge, he had no accomplices ; declared himself a republican, and that he made the attempt on the King because the latter had not kept his promises to the people, but had abandoned the free principles which raised him to the throne. Alibaud was often stopp'd in Ins defence by the King's attorney who forbade the use of similar language, he was led to execution with a black crape over his face, and barefooted, his execution caused little excitement at Paris. In England there appeared much less political excitement than our previous advices had led us to anticipate. In the house of Commons the Irish Church bill passed to a third reading in a very full house, by the small majority of 26 ; this lean majority has rather damped the spirits of the vvliigs, the Lords continued firm in their opposition to the great reform measures of the Commons. This state of affairs cannot long continue ; a new elec-

tion of the house of Commons is anticipated, to ascertain the present state of public opinion; both whigs and tories are sanguine that the result will be favorable to their respective hopes. In Spain the Carlists were much more active and displayed far more military talents than their opponents, the former had gained some advantages. General Evans remained in position before St. Sebastian, waiting the movements of Cordova þÿ the elections for the new Cortes was to soon take place, great hopes are entertained that a majority of Mendizibal's friends would be returned ; and that he would soon be reinstated as Premier. The average price of Muscovada Sugar July 10th in London, was 45 shillings in Bond, duty unpaid.

We have been favored with New York papers to August 11th þÿinclusive: The Indian war in Florida continued, and the Creeks and Cherokees had joined the Seminoles but the former had been mostly subdued, and large numbers of the Indians had been removed to the west of the Mississippi. In consequence of intrigues between the Mexicans, and the above tribes of Indians, General Gaines commanding the U. S. troops bad advanced to Nachitochez in Texas; (about 50 miles beyond the U. S. Frontier), to prevent any co-operation between the Mexicans and Indian tribes. The Texian army under Lamar is thought fully equal to cope with any force the Mexican government can send against them ;þÿ there are strong symptoms of revolution in Mexico, and of the overthrow of Santa Anna's party: the advance of the Mexican army under Urrea had been suspended, and it was supposed hostilities would not recommence for two or th ec months.

To Young Men. þÿ There is no moral object so beautiful to me as a conscientious young inan. I watch him a. I do a star in the heaven ; clouds may be oefore him, but we know that his light is behind them, and will beam again ; the blaze of others' prosperity may outshine him, but we know that, though unseen, he illumines his own true sphere He resists temptation not without, struggle, for that is not a virtue ; but he docs resist, and conquer ; he hears the sarcasm of the profligate, and it stings him þÿ for that is the trial of virtue þÿ but he heals the wound with his own pure touch. He heeds not the watchword of fushion if it leads to sin ; the Atheist who says not only in his heart, but with his lips, ' there is no God !' controls him not, for he sees the hand of a creating God and reveres it þÿ of a persevering God, and rejoices in it.

A gentleman of Liclifielil meeting the Doctor returning from a walk, enquired how far he had been ? The Doctor replied, he had gone round Mr. Levet's field (the place where the scholars play) in search of a rail that he used to jump over when a boy, "and' says the Doctor, in a transport of joy, I have been so fortunate as to find it : 1 stood gazing upon it some time with a degree of rapture, for it brought to my mind all my juvenile sports and pastimes, and at length, I determined to try my skill and dexterity ; 1 laid aside my hat and wig, pulled off my coat, and leaped over it twice. Thus the great Dr. Johnson, only three years before his death, was without his hat, wig, or coat, jumping over a rail he used to fly over when a schoolboy. þÿ Boswell's Life of Johnson.

A Fair Offer. þÿ Make a lull estimate of all you owe, and all that is owing you Re- þÿ duce the same to note. þÿ As fast as you collect pay over to those you owe ; it you can't collect, renew your note every year, and get the best security you can. Go to business diligently, and be industrious þÿ lose no time þÿ waste no idle moments be very prudent and þÿ economical in all things þÿ discard all pride but that of acting well þÿ be faithful in your duty to God by regular and hearty prayer morning and night þÿ attend church and meeting regularly every Sunday, and " do unto all men as you would they should do unto you." II you are too needy in your own circumstances, to give to the poor, do whatever you have in your power to do for them cheerfully but if þÿ you can, always help the worthy poor and unfortunate. Pursue this course diligently and sincerely for seven years, and it you are not happy, comfortable and independent in all your circumstances, come to me and I will pay your debts. Dr. Franklin. þÿ
