There is no greater argument in the world of our spiritual weakness, and the falseness of our hearts in matters of religion, than the backwardness most men have always and all men sometimes, to say their prayers, so weary of their length, so glad when they arc done, so ready to find an excuse, so apt to lose an opportunity. Diving Extraordinary. þÿ It appears from a Neapolitan paper called the Omnibus, that there is a wonderful diver in Naples, named Lorenzo Giordano, a native of Flumara, in Calabria, who is able to remain six hours under the water in the deepest places, and to walk at the bottom at the rate of a mile an hour. He has requested permission to be privileged for two years, and to have a third of all lie may find in his marine peregrination. If this permission be granted him, lie offers to be at the whole expcnce of the undertaking, and to make any experiments that may be considered necessary.

A pedant, on a voyage, being in danger of shipwreck, and seeing the other passengers catch hold of various articles on deck to keep them afloat, seized upon one of the anchors. Three persons, namely, a pedant, a bald man, and a barber, travelling together, agreed that, during the night, each should watch in his turn four hours, while the other two slept. The lot for the first watch fell to the barber. As soon as he saw his companions asleep, gently raising up the pedant, he shaved his head and presently afterwards awakened him. The pedant roused from his slumber, yawned scratched his head, and finding it smooth exclaimed, " what a stupid creature is this barber, he has waked the bald man instead of me."

There is something remarkable in the composition of the Jewish and Christian Scriptures, that, although in every language they are the easiest book to a learner, they are yet dignified, interesting, and impressive. The Pentateuch, Psalms, and Gospels, unite, in a singular degree, simplicity and perspicuity, with foice, energy, and pathos. I cannot satisfy myself what the literary peculiarities, the felicities of language are, which make them so universally comprehensive, and yet avoid insipidity, feebleness, and tedium ; which display so often such genuine eloquence and majesty, and yet are neither affected nor elaborate, nor, in general, above the understanding of the common reader. þÿ Turner's History of England.

Healthy Bodies. þÿ To have healthy bodies, people must go early to bed ; they must rise early in the morning; they must enjoy bodily exercise during a certain period of each day, and be exposed while taking that exercise to the direct influence of the solar light; and their minds are at no time so fitted to work, as during those hours, which, by nature's laws, are the proper hours for works ot all kinds.

What 1 like to see þÿ 1 like to see merchants and mechanics keep their shop doors and windows closed until the sun is an hour high ; it shows they are independent, and ask no favors of their customers. 1 like to see young women walking the streets on Sundays in their silks, with holes in their stockings ; it shows they are more attentive to things above than below. 1 like to see men crowding round the bar room Monday morning boiorc sunrise : it shows their anxiety to get to their week's employment in good season. I like to see women send their butter to market in a dirty cloth ; it shows ecouomy, as it saves washing. I like to see men pay their debts on the back of an execution ; it saves trouble hereafter. HOUSTON AT NEW ORLEANS. We extract the following interesting intelligence, from the New Orleans Bee ol the 23d ult. There can be no longer, any doubt of the sweeping victory of the Texians, and the successful establishment of their independence. Texas. þÿ In the schooner Flora, arrived at New Orleans on Sunday 22d ult. came passenger General Samuel Houston, commander in chief orthe Texiah Army, for the purpose of obtaining medical advice, badly wounded. By him we have tlie official confirmation of

the battle of the 21st ult. and the capture of Santa Anna. Former accounts are substantially correct. Santa Anna was at Velaseo under a stiong guard The army was left under the command of Rush, Secretary of War, who had been elected by the army Brigadier General. The Texian lorce had accumulated since the battle to 1800; and had advanced to and were crossing the Brazos, flushed with victory. The Mexican army under Seisma and others, had all concentrated and amounted to 2500 men, the remnant of 7000 who entered Texas. They were crossing the Colorado by rafts and swimming ; and were in the utmost confusion. Those who had escaped the battle of the 21st reported that it bad been fought by 5000 Texans Col. Burleson was close to the enemy with 200 cavalry, and they were retreating before him. 250 Mexicans surrendered after burying a piece of cannon, to 2 officers and 50 Texan soldiers. All was panic and confusion in the Mexican army. Santa Anna had oflered an armistice which had been refused, he had made further offers to acknowledge the independence of Texas, making Rio Grande the boundary line, and remaining a hostage until the government of the United States should consent to guarantee the treaty ; and it should be approved hv the Mexican Senate. Texas was cons dcred safe and the war ended; and the Mexican army would probable be totally destroyed. þÿ General Houston had a cane presented him by Santa Anna ; and aiso his saddle.

(From the Richmond Courier.) The Prince of Capua and Miss Penelope Smyth þÿ The following is an extract of a letter from the London Morning Herald, dated Madrid, Feb. 22. Four days since a travelling carriage, with, it was said, an English family, came in by the j Valencia road, and stopped at þÿGenie hotel, s in the Gallo de la Reyna þÿ The gentleman j was young and handsome ; the lady eminently so ; and both had all the appearance ol being of the first class of society. The arrival of an English lady at Madrid is rather an event, and every one was anxious to learn who our beautiful country woman was ; but a strange mystery seems to hang over the party ; and neither the gentleman nor his servants wmuld give their names at the hotel ; and when the Majordomo spoke of the police, they snapped their fingers, and said the police was not for them. The public curiosity was excited by all this, and still more so when it was known that M. Mendizabal had called twice and was closeted with the gentleman, and that two communications were passed to the Queen at the Pardo. I chanced to live at the same hotel, and the gossip of the servants found its way my to room ; and each day the wonder

still more grew, as there was no application made from the party at the English Legation, and it was uncertain even if they were a married couple, or lovers, or brother and sister, as they had separate chambers, the þÿlady s maid always sleeping in the same room with her mistress, and an upper servant, as com panion, in that of the master. þÿ Their appearance excited great interest, as he was a young man of 22, very handsome, tall, and well formed, though perhaps hair, not red, but bordering upon it, might be considered a defect ; and she was absolutely an angel, with a face full of beauty, deep blue eyes, lair hair, and a person without fault. For three days their secret was preserved, but at length an accident brought it to light, and we ha\e discovered in the young pair of w anderers, no less important personages than Prince Charles of Naples and Miss Penelope Smyth, about whose runaway match so much has been said and sung; and the funny part ol the story is, that rio one can tell whether they are married or come here to be married, or on the road to Gretna Green, where the blacksmith laughs at the threats of Kings as well as fathers. þÿ He is, however, a brother to the Queen- Kegent, and he perhaps comes to his sister f r advice, as she knows how to manage in equally difficult matters ; or perhaps, imagining that M. Mendizabal, by his vote of confidence, has the power to secure him the succession, notwithstanding the angr«fhis brother, and the rage of the Neapolitan people.

Miss Penelope Smyth is an Irish lady, who swept down in her time all the rural beaus in the county of Waterford, and I well recollect her at the Cork Assizes, with a train of feathers and a train of fops as long as Mr. I þÿO Connell stail. She afterwards levied hoand, as lady Morgan said, at the Cawstle, till not a heart w as left for others, or a husband for her. She then shot down

half Europe, till she shone in the eternal city, like the Goddess of Beauty come back to earth, and not a great man in Rome who did not | worship at her shrine. A duel took place on j her account on the Neapolitan froniier, be- //. MA TTIIIESEJV. i tween an English gentleman and an Italian Nobleman, in w hich the latter was killed ; and it was the pistols of the Prince Charles, which he had lent to the Englishman, which had shot the Duke ; his name was called in question, and from his name his heart, till every one saw that the legitimate succession was about to be endangered. On this Miss Penelope Smyth, who had come over to Naples, was advised by the police to return to Romo; which hint she took, but Prince Charles quickly followed her, and one bright day both were found wanting, and were not heard of till they reached Florence, from whence they went to Switzerland, and have come by way of Marseilles, to Valencia and Madrid to create a sensation, and to divide the publ,c attention from the projects of the Government.

Some people say that this marriage is M. Mendizabal's grand secret, and that the Prince has just reached in time to reveal it to the Cortes, while others hint that he has come to keep his sister in countenance, and that the menage of the Prince of Capua and Miss IVnelojre Smyth is intended as a pendant to the domestic manners o( the Queen and M. .Munos. Whatever may be the result, no one can deny that the Prince is a handsome, spirited young fellow, who gives up, probnblv a throne, for the lady of his love, and that Mis# Penelope Smyth is as beautiful as the day.

From the Monthly Magazine. TRICKS UPON TRAVELLERS. A Yankee Trick. It was a time of great bustle and expectation in the village of L , þÿ somewhere out of the world and up in the þÿwoods, in the State of Massachusetts. There was to be a special frolic in the shape of a horse race þÿ a horse race, do I say ? 1 mean a scramble of quadrupeds, for since the practice had been known there, very few of the animals that put their hoofs in, would have been entitled to the name and honors of a horse, at Doncaster. Four footed animals they were for the most part, though some of the fourth in reserve, and chose to go upon three þÿ Narraganset pacers, Vermont stumblers, Berkshire blunderers, Connecticut caperers, Worcester plough-joggers, Dog- town dumpies þÿ in short, the tag-rag and bob tail of the four footed creation; not that Yankee-land is deficient in prime horse flesh ; witness the Tom Thumb the great, or the steeds of the mail stages, if you have been in that country ; or the progeny of that celebrated marc whom a flash of lightning chased round a ten acre lot, without being able to catch her. But horse-racing is no regular trade or common occupation in New England: nobody makes a business of rearing animals for the turf ; and when an occurrence of this sort takes place, it is no very studied affair, but a frolicsome scramble among all the beasts of burden in the neighborhood, or such as chance brings along at the moment. Once a year it had been customary to run a race of this sort in the village of L ,

and the fleetest runner of this motley multitude, won a prize of some value, to which every adventurer contributes a sum. On the present occasion the prize was considerably augmented by an offer from an individual, who constituted himself a society for the promotion of horse racing, and more than common interest was of course excited on the approach of the festival. The old farmers who had horses for running, gave them extra quantities of corn, and fewer applications of the lash, as if to be fat and fleet was the same thing. Some however, were more cautious in their preparations, and, among the rest, Job Hawker, a sly, calculating, guessing, questioning, bargaining, swapping, Jack-ofall-trades sort' of a chap, long sided and limber tongued ; with a face as grave as a deacon, but a roguish twinkle of the eye on

But while he was flattering himself with the prospect of a certain victory, and as the day of trial approached, he was thrown into consternation by the arrival of a stranger, mounted on a Canadian poney, who came with the avowed intention of putting in for the prize. At the first announcement of this intelligence Job fell into despair, for it so happened that he knew the individual, having encountered him in the north part of Vermont, while on a trading excursion in that quarter. Job had witnessed a trial of speed which the poney exhibited there, and knew that his own Bucephalus was no match for him. It was plain that if the Canadian took a share in the race, he must win, and the catastrophe seemed inevitable, for nobody had a right to exclude him. It was a grievous thing to Job to think of having the prize snatched from before his eyes, when it had been augmented to a double value, and just at the moment when he imagined it within his grasp. Job had not all the patience of his namesake of old as evinced by his conduct in this emergency. He did not sit down and curse the day he was born, giving up the whole concern for a bad bargain, but he sat

down on a log of wood and scratched his head. The sage manoeuvre was practised for the purpose of devising by what device, or quizzical circumvention, he might get rid of this formidable rival. His first thought was to inveigle him into a swap, but it would require a great deal of palavering and chaffering and must prove a long job þÿ too long for what little time remained. He then thought of buying him off from the enterprize, giving him a bird in the hand for two in the bush; but this would cost too much, and Job was resolved to have the whole or none. His third project was to frighten or obstruct the poney by some preconcerted accident, just at the time of setting out ; but this did not appear, on consideration, to be just the thing. Evening drew on þÿ the next morning was to bring all parties upon the turf þÿ and there was not a moment to be lost. Job had cudgelled his brain for two hours to no purpose ; he started up in a great puzzle, and began to wend his way homeward. As he reached the little green in front of the meeting house, he heard a loud huzzaing ; he looked up and beheld a crowd of people following a fat ox, with a flag upon his horns. At this instant a thought struck him ; he did not shout cuieka, but it was because he knew no Greek. Early the next morning, on that hint he acted. How sincere and ardent is the love of Woman ! how pure the throbbings of her heart ! how earnest the devotedness of her attachment ! Do pain and sickness oppress her, with what fortitude does she suffer ! Do poverty and want attend her, she bears with patience the miseries of her lot ! GALVESTON ISLAND, Oth MAY, 1830. The particulars of the battle with Santa Anna, will probably have already reached you as however the presence of Santa Anna and his officers here have placed me in posession of particulars not generally known, and as besides every circumstance connected with this memorable event is of vivid interest, I dare say the details I am about to give you will be found worthy attention. Santa Anna had just fired New Washington, when news reached him on the 20th, ot the appearance of Texiari troops. He was taken completely by surprise and says that as he had found all the farms deserted, and could learn nothing of General Houston, he concluded all the inhabitants had left the country. A skirmish only took place on the 20th with a small detachment or scouting party, Houston keeping the main body in the woods under a hill where none could be seen. The next day, the 21st, St Anna was quietly taking his siesta, when he was awoke by his aid with news of our approach, which he swore was a d þÿ d lie. General Cos had arrived after a forced march with a re-inforcement about an hour or two before and was likewise taking his siesta. þÿ Some of the men were sleeping, some cooking, some washing, in short in any situation but that of preparation for battle, when they were pounced upon by us at about 4 þÿo clock P. M. of the 21st. Our troops marched up in front of the enemy on the open praire, never firing a musket or rifle until within 80 yards. The enemy were posted behind breastworks, and in the

woods, and commenced with their artillery at a distance of 400 yards. Our artillery opened at 210 yards. When the charge was sounded we rushed upon them ; the cry of þÿ the Alamo and La þÿBahia resounding throughout the lines. Their artillery (one piece only) was taken loaded, and when in the act of being primed, and every artillerist put to the sword who did not fly. The battle lasted 19 minutes and then commenced the rout and slaughter. The poor devils of Mexicans would hold up their hands, cross themselves, and sing out me no þÿAlamo, but nothing could save them ; the blood of our countrymen was too fresh in the memory of our people to let one Mexican escape, until worn down with pursuit and slaughter, they commenced making prisoners, t Xlicers and all fled ; none dare attempt to st' m the torrent. The Mexicans threw down their guns loaded, and sought safety in every direction, while our cavalry and infantry pursued and cut them down. Muskets and rifles were clubbed when they had not lime to re" I i<i, and the brains of the Mexicans beat out i as they came up with them. The captain of one of the companies of regulars pointed out one of his men to me who fired 19 rounds and used three muskets, two of them having got choaked, and he having broke their breeches off over the heads of the Mexicans. The battle was fought just above a place marked on the map lithographed last summer, in New York, þÿMc Cormicks The enemy þÿ þÿ were driven and retreated, until many were forced into the water, which you will see

bounds the land there. They ran in up to their nocks, and our riflemen would shoot them in the head. Santa Anna and Almonte in flying, plunged their horses into a quagmire, were thrown off and nearly suflbeated before extricated, Both continued their flight on

foot. Santa Anna was furnished with a fresh horse on which he escaped ten miles further, and was taken next day in disguise. Almonte, finding all was lost, and fearing all would be cut to pieces, placed himself at the head of 3 or 400 men, made them form in column, four or 8 deep, throw down their arms, and then held up a white flag and surrendered them at once to a small body of our troops who were in pursuit, and they were all marched into camp together. S anta Anna was not recognized until presented to General Houston, whom he complimented highly, by saying þÿ « The man who conquered the Napoleon of the South was born to no common þÿdestiny. ' With Santa Anna all his staff were taken or killed. Il any escaped, it was a captain of cavalry, and it is supposed about ten others. There never was so complete a defeat with so little loss on one side. Ours consisted of 3 killed on the field of battle 5 dead since of their wounds, and 15 more wounded: in all 23 killed and wounded. The Mexican dead were strew'ed around lor ten miles, and must have amounted to at least 900 ; as many or more ore prisoners. Almonte says there were 1200 Mexican troops in the engagement, the best they had. We made the attack with less than 000 men. All Santa þÿAnna camp s equipage, baggage every kind, ef in short, all the Mexicans had with them, fell into our hands ; some 8 or 810,000 in specie. There was supposed to have been 850,000 in cash in the army chest. The gold part of it disappeared very soon. Some of the troops had

line pickings. Galveston Island, 8th May, 1830. We have all the Mexican prisoners here, consisting of the President Santa Anna, General Cos, Almonte, and a number of Generals, Colonels, >k.c. &c 1 enclose you a list of them, their ages, &lc. as also of the officers killed in battle þÿ the officers made it out themselves for me. These prisoners, as I expected all came down in the first steamboat alter I left camp and were landed last evening. þÿ Santa Anna, Almonte and Secretaries have been placed on board an armed schooner in the harbor. The Mexican troops are running out of Texas much faster than they came in. Thirty men who went on with Santa þÿAnna s express came up with 200 Mexicans with 9 pieces artillery of and they immediately surrendered saying if Santa Anna and the officers were taken, there was no use in their fighting. General Wall, a Frenchman, came in from another division of the army and surrendered himself. He said he did not wish to fight any more if St Anna was taken. He has been released and sent back. 1 send with this a duplicate of St. þÿAnna sletter to Filasola. He handed it to me with a request that I would endeavour to forward it but as there is no chance that I shall be able to do this, I send it to you as a curiosity. The Mexican dead lie yet unburied and the stench in the neighbourhood is intolerable. Galveston Island, 10th May, 1830. I have this moment parted with Santa Anna and Almonte who the Cabinet take with them to Velasco, which, for a while will be

the seat of government. They are both under great apprehension for their personal safety_though 1 have no doubt their lives will be spared þÿ and disliked leaving here very much. Santa Anna embraced me in the most cordial and affecting Mexican manner on parting. þÿ He and Almonte were kept on board the Invincible until the moment of their departure.

Notwithstanding his cruelties, I could not help pitying the President of Mexico, as I escorted him from the side of the vessel to the steamboat. His eyes were suffused with tears. þÿ The steamboat was crowded to overflowing þÿ music playing a quick American air þÿ smiling faces all around, even among the lowest classes, who had lost their all.

MAKKIAGE OF T1IE QUEEN OF PORTUGAL. Lisbon, April 9. þÿ The long expected husband of our young Queen arrived here yes terday, and the marriage of this youthful bride and bridegroom was celebrated to-day, in the cathedral, with some show, though 1 cannot say a great deal, of pomp and ceremony. þÿ The cannon from the Castle at Belem, and at St. þÿGeorsre s Castle announced that the Manchester steamer, with his Highness on board, was entering the Tagus, and might be expected to anchor in a short time. The whole of the city, and, I may say, the river, was thrown into agitation. In a few minutes he came to land, and this fine young man received the first Portuguese welcome, as he passed slowlv along the line to the place where his cai riage was in waiting. To you, who have so lately seen him, a description of his person will be unnecessary, but I must say, the impression his first appearance made here was most favourable, and every one began to augur 'veil from his fine gentlemanly presence and unaffected manner. He wore the uniform of a Portuguese General, but he was attended bv two officers of his own country in their national uniform, and a gentleman in a plain dress, said to be his chaplain. The people received him well, and took ofi their hats, and, as he passed by them, he repeatedly bowed to them, touching his hat, and appearing inclined often to take it ofl in return for their civility. Something like a struggle between habitual good nature and the necessity of being dignified was evident ; and his anxious, laughing

blue eye contradicted the would be gravity of his countenance. The fair hair escaped in curls under his hat, and the brightness of his complexion and the slightness of his figure, made him look even younger than he really is ; and he seemed to me, as he walked through the line of sworthy Portuguese, with premature seriousness on his brow, like a school-boy playing part private theatricals, a in and doing majesty and dignity. In my heart I pitied the poor youth, removed from the honesty and sincerity of a German Court to tins bothed of intrigue and deceit. However, his fate is scaled, and God grant that he may be happy and prosperous, in spite of all the gloomy lbrebodings which the fate of his predecessor and the wretched position of this country inspire. He left the arsenal in the royal carriage, and passed along the street, where the people were in crowds to receive him, to the Palace of the Necessidadcs, almost at the other end of the town.

The Queen, whose anxiety may be wel| conceived waited with impatience in the balcony of the Palace, from whence she could see the steamer as it came in, and witness all the honours paid to her young husband ; and when the cannon announced he had touched the land, her eyes were anxiously turned in the direction lie was to come. At length the cheers of the people announced his close approach, and she, like a young creature as she is, stooped down to get a good peep at him through l he iron bars of the balcony, saluting him eagerly with her fan and hand, while he took oft' his hat and returned with gallantry her impatient and warm welcome. He then left the carriage, while she ran in from the window, and the husband and wife met for the first time. What their mutual feelings were Heaven alone can tell. She saw before her a fine, manly youth, such as even the romance of a girlish heart could desire, while

Still, she was a Queen, and Portugal was her dower ; and though fat and fair, she was not 40, but 17, and the eye of a lad of 19 is not very critical. However, they met and dined together, and then the Prince returned to his steamer, while the Queen remained at the Palace to weep her last þÿwidow tears, s and prepare for the coming happy day that was to give her a consort and her people a Prince. At 12 þÿo clock to-day the sound of cannon gave notice that the Queen had lelt the Palace, on which the Prince hastened from the steamer, and disembarked at the Exchange-square, proceeded to the cathedral ; but unfortunately his movements were too rapid, or those ol her Majesty too slow, and when he arrived at the great door her carriage had not come up, and he had to wait more than half an hour, evidently to his discomfort and to those about him, who sympathized with the anxiety of so young a bridegroom expecting the lady of his love. A certain numbar of Peers in their robes and of General Officers had met him at the steps of the Cathedral, and one, more considerate than the rest, had brought a seat lor the Prince, where he sat uncovered for some time ; but his patience and temper being exhausted, he put on his hat at iast, and then at this ease waited for his Royal Consort, whose

near approach the din of the accompanying crowds now gave notice of. It was one þÿo clock before her Majesty arrived, and then a train of noble ladies iiaving gone forth to receive her, and the Prince having joined her at the Cathedral steps, a procession was formed, headed by the Patriarch of Lisbon, who was to perform the marriage ceremony, and in the centre ot which, under a canopy of white silk, appeared the youthlul couple, the bridegroom holding her Majesty's hand in his, and bowing to the line ol noble, diplomatic naval, and military personages that welcomed their arrival. The Prince looked remarkably well, his slight tall frame strongly contrasting with the ample bulk of her Majesty. The Queen was also in her best smiles, a magnificent coronet of brilliants encircling her head, and many many yards of while satin her person.

They walked slowly up the aisle, Ins countenance being more grave than hers, until they reached the altar, where the Patiiarch gave them his benediction, and she was placed for a moment in the Chair of State, while the Prince stood on her left hand. They both then knelt down, and the ceremony of the mass was commenced, at a given period of which the Prince and the Queen were led again to the altar, and there, in the face of Heaven and of man, their hands were joined their vows were plighted, and they were made man and wife, their uniled ages being 3(5. The old Patriarch gave them his blessing, and the organ and the choir chaunted the prayers of the church lor their happiness, and the service of the mass was resumed, and the young couple again knelt down and concluded their devotions and mingled their sighs and their prayers on the same cushion. At length, the ceremony being concluded, the couple, now bound together for life, returned in the same order as they came, his countenance still bearing the same impenetrable gravity, while hers seemed to be affected by the so-

þÿ ynrvri .sr» lemnity of his, and was much more serious than it habitually is. The state coach, a very handsome aflair, drawn by magnificent English horses, was drawn up, and the bride and bridegroom, placed side by side, commenced their first matrimonial excursion, and returned to the Palace of the Necessidades, the bands of the several regiments playing constitutional airs, the National Guards presenting arms and the people receiving them with decorum, if not with enthusiasm, as they passed. Soon after their arrival at the Palace they appeared in one of the balconies, and the whole of the National Guard, about 8,000 men defiled before them ; but I did not hear one cheer, and, though the Prince had his hat off, the people in the Palace square were not uncovered. I am certain that the Queen was not a little annoyed at the coolness of her faithful subjects, and I fear the Prince was ruminating more than a young lad should on the strangeness of his position, as I observed them closely, and as they did not exchange a word, and were more reserved than the occasion required, or was natural for so young a pair. There is an air of gallantry and attention common on those occasions which the Prince did not put on, and the Queen seemed, like a young creature, at a loss to know how to act towards a gentleman who played his part with so much formality. Though the church is not a place for conversation, yet no bridegroom allows the marriage to pass without a few words of tenderness to his bride, and during the long

tedious ceremony which followed, an occasional short dialogue might be excused ; but I attentively observed the Prince and the Queen from their entrance to the church till their departure from it, and I do not think they spoke twice during the two hours ; and subsequently, when they stood at the balcony, they preserved the same forboding silence, though certainly the magnificence of the scenery, the splendor of the river, with ships of all nations upon it, must have been to him full of interest, independent of all those topics which the peculiarity of their situation would naturally give rise to. It is possible that youth and diffidence restrained both, and a husband of 19, a man before he is a boy, and a girl of 17, maid, wife, widow, and wife again, in the course of one year, may be overpowered by timidity and the novelty of their feelings, and every one will be anxious to assign some amiable reason for their composure ; but of the fact there can be no doubt, and of many marriages which I have seen 1 never saw a bride and bridegroom less at ease or more grave than this young and Royal couple. Lisbon April 1 1 þÿ Jt is with great pleasure I find that the melancholy which overhun the marriage and (list reception of the young 1 lincc and the more youthlul Queen has passed away, and that it is now evident, from their appearance in public, that they are as happy together as any couple can bo expected to be. At twelve o'clock yesterday they had to attend the Cortes, for the purpose of

the Queen proroguing the session in person, and the reserve which chilled them and the people interested in their welfare had given way ; and her Majesty was all smiles and good humour, while the Prince looked as sly and as happy as bridegroom should be. Indeed, she was more than smiles, for it was downright laughing, and her mirth at one moment almost burst her bodice, on seeing one of the old Chamberlains stumble and tumble while engaged in some formal piece ol

miTsx ccrcmonv ; while the Prince, with a wicked expression lurking in the corner of the eye, seemed to enjoy the fall, the old man being discomposed, not hurt, the outbreak of his þÿwife g s ood humour, and all the pomp and nonsencc he was taking a part in. The Queen sat on the throne while she read the closing Address, and the Prince sat than on her left, in a chair placed a little lower hers, and they were attended by the Ministers and courtiers in grand gala, while the Diplomatic Corps, and crowds of strangers and of the people, filled the tribunes and public galleries to an overflow. They both appeared at the Opera in the evening, and, of course, every place was occupied before their arrival. The concourse was immense, and really the Portuguese ladies made a fine show in five tiers of boxes, with plumes and feathers, and flowers and brilliants, and all the improvement of dress which the Constitution has brought with þÿit. The Marchioness de Louie, a Princess of the blood, a beautiful creature, was arrayed with a costly head-dress of diamonds, while the Countess of Fcrrobo, one of the richest of the modern nobility, rivalled both her and the Queen, with a plumage of brilliants worth 40,0001. The Queen, the Prince, and the Empress entered the Royal box at nine þÿo in clock, and they were received, I must say, the warmest manner ; three distinct rounds o applause were given, last, the to be sure, promoted by some mad-cap English midshipman who would have one cheer more ; and the

boxes were instantly hung with wreaths of flowers and garlands ot evergreen, and the orchestra played the Constitutional Hymn, and all the singers came forward with grand chorus, and gave a new hymn composed for the occasion. The Queen was delighted, and she laughed and smiled, and laughed again, while the Prince bowed, and placed his hand to his heart, and said with the immortal Shakespeare, þÿ Gentlemen, 1 thank you, while the dear Empress looked like an angel, and every one thought what a pity it was that she is a widow. They then sat down, the Prince being between the Queen and the Empress 5 and the young rogue played his part to perfection to both ladies, keeping his own wile in a continual roar of laughing, and provoking the sweet smile of his beautilul aunt. 1 he opera was the Exile oj Home, but, though a German, and of course a musician, 1 am certain the Prince did not hear a single note, and as to her Majesty, her ear was employed in listening to her lord's soil voice, and it was a chance if her own hearty peals ol laughing did not drown the violoncello, the double bass and all. A merrier trio have seldom met in a Royal box, and the harmoncy ol their circle seemed communicated to the house, for, instead of the formal cold audience which met on her þÿMajesty s birth day, every one now smiled, and was happy, and every thing passed off well except the opera, the pritna donna, the tenor, and the base being unable to make head against such a torrent of good humour. The

Queen wore her daidem of brilliants, and an ample robe of white satin, while the Prince, who appeared in the dress of the National Guard in the morning at the Cortes had resumed his General's costume in the evening, and looked as handsome as an Adonis in uniform. 1 cannot tell how the empress was dressed, for who, in looking at her sweet face, could pay attention to a toilette ? but she wore a smile which won every heart, and her eyes were her brilliants, her teeth her pearls, nnd her lips her rubies.

A ballet was given after the first act of the opera, at the close ol which the Royal party retired, the audience rising up and giving them a final cheer. An officer of the Guards who has lately had the honor of dining frequently at court, has given us the following account of the domestic habits there:þÿ At dinner there was much French spoken, but more German, which the Queen utters with clear rapidity and much gesticulation, frequently quoting from the poetical and prose writers in that language. Her amiable consort has something cheerful to say to every guest, with an extraordinary power of remembering names and events which interest the parties addressed. He is a hearty laugher, and enjoys a gay anecdote extremely, being good a raconteur himself. After dinner the Queen enjoys herself with the German worsted work, of which she is now engaged in executing a laborious pattern, the gentlemen standing around her table and conversing w hile she works. Our informant was very much struck by her relerence to the opinions and principles of Queen Charlotte, more especially when the young Prince of P inquired as to some points of etiquette in this country ; among others he asked, þÿ how was the line drawn as to receiving or excluding anv female whose conduct was said to be þÿquestionable? The Queen replied, It was the rule of the late Queen, that if a þÿlady s character was impeached before marriage, the Court was not to know any thing of her actions as long as she lived under her þÿhusband roof s ; once leaving that protection, under any pretence, after having excited observation by her conduct, no circumstances could reinstate her in her former position in

þÿsociety. The P added, þÿ And in the case of divorced persons Madam þÿ? The reply was, þÿ The Queen disapproved of this proceeding so much, that, although she publicly received some persons thus situated, they were never admitted to her private þÿparties. The P e inquired when the new Palace was to be inhabited, and was answered, þÿ I wish it as soon as possible, and constantly go to superintend its decoration. I quite love my rooms there and those charming gardens. During the evening the King played cribbnge and whist with some of tiic veteran companions of his early days, but constantly mixed in the conversations around, relating adventures which had occurred to him and his family. He always uses the words þÿ my þÿlather, or þÿ my þÿmother, instead of the more formal titles, giving an impression of natural affection in the allusions to them. Politics were never once introduced, and persons of all parties were invited together. The dress of the Queee in private is as plain as possible, generally a simple light silk; and she wears very few ornaments, except her rings, which are always of great value and beauty. She is much paler than last year, and in figure considerably slighter. Her consort seems in excellent health, occasionally disposed to sleep after dinner, a habit he much dislikes, and dreads its increase with his years. þÿ Guiana Chronicle June 17.

A writer in the Woonsocket Patriot, states that in 1794, while spinning a quantity of sea island cotton, the evenness and beauty of the yarn attracted the attention of Mrs. Slater, and the question arose whether if doubled and twisted, it would not make good sewing thread. The experiment was tried, and in order to be fully satisfied with the result, a sheet was made, one half with linen, and the other half with cotton thread, and immediately put into use. The cotton wore the best and the linen was the first that was rent. From this period, Mr.

Slater commenced the manufacture of cotton thread, and it soon spread into England, France, and all other European countries, where it is generally supposed to be of English origin þÿ though the credit of the invention belongs almost entirely to an American matron. þÿ American Paper.

By the arrival of tho schooner Atalunta ycsteriiay, from Tampico, we have received the journal of that place up to the 13th instant ; but private letters have been received in town to the 19th. These latter communicate the information that when the defeat and capture of Santa Anna had become known there, the Subalterns of the Army and Government had threatened to massacre all foreigners found in the place ; but that the British Vice Consul, and the American Consul, having remonstrated with the military commandant of Tampico, he used precautionary measures to prevent disturbances. An English corvette of war being then in port and about to sail, the Vice Consul prevailed on the captain to delay his departure, to act as a protection for the British residents. But four or five days had elapsed between the intelligence of Santa þÿAnna cap- s ture and the sailing of the Atalanta, and all continued quiet. The Gaceta de Tomaulipas contains little positive information as to the affairs in Mexico, nor any' remarks on events, except that about 4,000 men had been raised at San Luis de Potosi, to enter Texas, after learning the defeat of Santa þÿAnna army s ; but it does not appear by whom these troops were levied or commanded. The Atalanta brought a rumor that the ports of Tospan, Tampico, and Metamoras would be closed to American commerce. It is feared that non-intercourse of this kind will become meral throughout the Mexican coast ;

and it is not a matter of surprise, for if it would have been proper for the United States to resolve on non-intercourse with France, from the non-fulfilment of a treaty, equally proper must it be for Mexico to declare nonintercourse with the United States for nonefnlfilment of the treaty of alliance and neutrality. Our merchants will then he obliged to resort to Havana as an entrepot for their Mexican trade from Europe and this country; and so materially injure the commerce of New Orleans. It is known that in 1830 there were 15,000 American citizens resident in the Mexican Republic, for the purposes of trade, independent of the inhabitants of Texas, and it is now believed that there are upwards of þÿ 20,000. These must necessarily be at the mercy of the Mexican authorities, should they choose to exercise revengeful feelings for the interference evinced by the United States in the affairs of Texas. It were almost well that congress followed the example of the British Parliament, by passing a foreign enlistment act; so that a pacific treaty of alliance or neutrality with a friendly nation were not one of name only, but of reality. How otherwise can a treaty be enforced? þÿ Bee.
